fields.country: Nicaragua (San Sebastian de Yali municipality, Jinotega department)
fields.subnational_unit: San Sebastian de Yali municipality (74 rural communities; five communities reported in the paper)
fields.population: rural households in five communities, split into those served by community-based water committees (CAPS) and self-provided households
fields.sample_size: data collected in all 74 communities of the municipality (about 22,500 people); the paper reports a case study of five communities with 296 households (the text gives 154 served by CAPS and 149 not served, which sums to 303, an inconsistency in the paper); a border case has 7 self-provided families
fields.study_design: methodological case study: stratified household survey (CAPS-served versus self-provided strata, exact binomial confidence limits with finite-population correction) measuring access against the normative content of the human right to water (availability, physical accessibility, quality, affordability, acceptability)
fields.effect_measure: descriptive indicators by stratum (service-level scores on nine indicators; coliform classes); no inferential estimate of an institutional effect
fields.effect_estimate: Faecal contamination: among self-provided households about 64% used sources above 10 CFU/100 ml, 20% between 0 and 10 and about 16% had none; among households served by CAPS 0%, 82% and 18%. High contamination is therefore worse for self-provided households, but the share drinking coliform-free water is similar in both groups. The authors conclude the stratified design locates minority sub-groups that central-tendency indicators hide, at higher field cost that they judge feasible, and that data should be disaggregated for local, national and global monitoring (JMP post-2015).
fields.section: Full text (journal article): Introduction; Case study; Methodology; Results and discussion; Conclusions
fields.exact_location: Case study section (SSY municipality, five communities, 296 households); Tables 3-4 (indicators, sample-size design); results on contamination by subgroup; Conclusions

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a methodological case study in one Nicaraguan municipality (five communities) on measuring disparities in access to water against right-to-water criteria; descriptive, no estimate of a legal or institutional effect; read in full text 2026-10-04.
pdf_note: Flores, Jimenez and Perez-Foguet 2016 (Social Indicators Research), full text read in Drive file S285_Flores_Baquero_2016...pdf; tables read as text
notes: ELIGIBILITY NOTE: the paper tests a measurement method; its link to legal or institutional barriers is the right-to-water framing and the committee-managed (CAPS) versus self-provision distinction. Criterion 3 and the institutional fit are arguable.
